item.title: 5 characteristics of top-performing SOC agents
item.description:
CrowdStrike has seen customers use our no-code agent-building workspace, Charlotte AI AgentWorks, to build thousands of AI agents. We’ve been fascinated by how they are designed and which ones become top-performing agents invoked hundreds or thousands of times in daily operations. Below are the design properties these agents share.

What top-performing security agents have in common

      1. Surgical scope

      These agents solve a specific, measurable problem. They do one thing very well, and their output informs broader workflows.

      Most organizations start by designing a general-purpose security assistant to address a range of tasks; however, these assistants are challenging to deploy and measure. Even if it can get to a working state, it can easily drift from its objective in dynamic enterprise environments. An agent with a narrow, well-defined job is more likely to become critical infrastructure because its output is predictable and trustworthy enough to measure, test, and build around.

      2. Multi-agent pipelines

      They are also typically cheaper to run, for two structural reasons.

      The first is model assignment. In a monolith, the whole task inherits whatever model its single hardest step requires. Every trivial step is then paid for at that rate. Decomposing the task lets each stage run on the optimal model applicable to the agent, and even allows delegating structured tasks to automated scripts or applications that don’t require AI models.

      The second is context. A single long-running agent accumulates history, and every subsequent step spends resources to carry it. But an agent pipeline hands each stage only the input that stage needs. A failed stage can also be retried on its own rather than rerunning the entire investigation.

      3. An explicit specification of what is not allowed

      Top-performing agents often include explicit instructions outlining what the agent can and cannot do. This guardrail ensures the agent behavior is bounded. Without it, an agent asked to triage an alert may decide to query adjacent systems, draw conclusions outside its remit, or take actions nobody sanctioned. The guardrail also complements other controls including role-based access, authorized tools, and invocability.

      4. A built-in fail-safe

      An agent won’t always reach a confident answer. Rather than guess, it should be instructed to escalate ambiguity.

      The design response to address this has two parts. One, build a clear escalation path, such as instructing the agent to “flag for analyst review” whenever the agent identifies a circumstance as inconclusive. Additionally, build a checkpoint for the agent, such as a sample of closed cases, or a second agent whose job is to validate the first to catch the cases it doesn’t flag.

      5. Strictly defined output

      The highest invoked agents are part of fully automated pipelines instead of ending up in chat, which requires structured inputs and outputs.

      This differs from how most people imagine enterprise AI. The conversational interface makes an agent demonstrable, but it also prevents the agent from becoming part of a defined SecOps workflow. A chat response is consumed by a human who interprets it. A structured verdict, such as a schema with defined fields, bounded lengths, and an explicit decision, can be consumed by a ticketing system, a containment workflow, or the next agent in the pipeline. Structured output allows agents to be chained.

      Building top-performing agents

      Start with the right problem

      The problem sets up every design decision. The best candidates are high-volume, repeatable tasks with just enough nuance to require reasoning and judgment. Crucially, these can’t be easily addressed with deterministic automation or a script. Existing documented playbooks, or a sequence of steps analysts consistently follow, are great insertion points for an agent.

      The task must be narrow enough that its output can be measured and verified. The ability to measure agent impact makes a performance feedback loop possible. It provides a clear way to check whether an output is correct, and whether an edit to the agent helped or hurt.

      Choose the right model and test it

      Identify the model suited to the task and compare accuracy, speed, and cost across other models. In practice, this can result in an optimal allocation of tools. Matching capability to task optimizes system performance while accounting for costs, latency, and compliance requirements.

      Refine instructions

      Define what is in scope. Supply context, knowledge files, and organizational context or policies. Specify exceptions, fail-safe procedures, and what to do in inconclusive scenarios.

      Optimize output

      Work backward from your agent’s handoff in a broader workflow. How does output need to be structured to be consumed by the receiving analyst or tool? Define character limits, required output schema, and tuning required for downstream handoffs.

      Implement measurable performance

      As part of agent design and governance, implement a means of validating and tracking agent performance — outputting content in a database for human review, conducting a sampling of agent outputs for assessments, or conducting agent testing against a validated data set.

      Expand tooling and actions gradually

      Measurable agent performance enables security teams to take a phased approach to autonomy, with each stage earned through demonstrated reliability. A common progression begins with summarization: The agent reports; the human decides and acts. Next comes recommendation, where the agent proposes a course of action but the human owns the decision. From there, agents move to approval-gated execution, deciding and staging an action for human approval, and ultimately to full automation, acting independently while humans review later.

item.title: The same AI question emits more carbon dioxide in Texas than in Sweden
item.description:
The Swedish AI company Berget AI, together with researchers from the Stockholm Environment Institute (SEI) and the organizations WattTime and Klimatkollen, has developed a new method for calculating how much carbon dioxide different AI requests generate.

The aim is to make the AI ​​industry’s climate impact more transparent and give companies the opportunity to compare different suppliers.

According to the method, for example, a typical request to the AI ​​model Kimi K3 results in around 0.4 grams of carbon dioxide emissions in Sweden, 1.6 grams in Ireland, 2.5 grams in Germany, and 3.2 grams in Texas. Despite identical hardware.

Berget AI has published the method as open source, meaning other companies can freely use it. A web-based calculator also makes it possible to compare emissions between different AI models and geographical regions.

item.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
item.description:
Private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised, allowing attackers to forge certificates for any site. The keys were revealed due to low entropy, not through a known breach. Browsers blocked them using revocation lists, but other software had to remove the emSign ECC G3 root. Unpatched systems remain exposed to forged certificates, including client auth and mTLS.

By Chris Swan

item.title: Netflix Bridges AWS IAM and Internal Identity with Workload Attestation
item.description:
Netflix has developed a workload attestation mechanism for Apache Spark jobs running on Amazon EMR. The design combines AWS IAM identity with signed claims from Netflix’s control plane before issuing short-lived internal X.509 certificates, allowing managed compute workloads to authenticate to internal services without directly injecting credentials.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: 3 ways to get your data ready for AI
item.description:
Most enterprise data was designed to be consumed by people. But automation and AI agents will soon make up a much larger share of the workforce. KPMG’s Global Tech Report predicts that digital assistants will account for 36% of core technology teams’ capacity by 2027, up from 28% in 2025.

This is why data readiness has risen to the top of technology leaders’ priority lists. In a separate KPMG survey, 58% of leaders cited data readiness and access as one of their biggest challenges to deploying AI agents.

Data that works for reports and dashboards can create problems for AI. Definitions may differ across the business, with data stored separately from the rules governing its use.

Preparing for an AI workforce starts with making enterprise data searchable, contextual, and trusted.

Three steps to AI-ready data

1. Make enterprise data searchable.

AI agents need to identify which data to use and where to find it across multiple data products and technology environments.

An ontology maps business concepts to the data associated with them. When an agent receives a question or action, it breaks the request into relevant domains and concepts. The ontology then identifies which data products and assets contain the information it needs.

Consider a wealth advisor asking an AI assistant about a customer’s recent branch interactions to identify potential cross-sell opportunities. Answering might require pulling product data from one data platform and branch experience data from another entirely.

2. Give AI the context it needs.

AI also needs to understand what enterprise data means. Let’s say you ask AI: “What’s our best-selling product in the mid-market segment?” The answer hinges on how the business defines “best-selling” – by units, revenue, or margin – and which accounts qualify as “mid-market.”

Knowledge engineering captures and makes this organizational context available to AI. It does this through:

  • technical metadata: identifies what data exists and how it flows through systems
  • semantics: define business terms, definitions, and synonyms
  • ontologies: establish relationships among business concepts
  • knowledge graphs: connect those relationships to enterprise information

These elements help AI interpret data using the same business meaning employees apply to it. Knowledge engineering can also incorporate institutional knowledge that agents can draw on when making autonomous decisions.

3. Build trust into AI-ready data.

AI agents need to make decisions from authoritative, governed data. Existing data controls provide a good starting point.

Enterprises also need to determine whether an agent inherits the access privileges of the person using it or receives its own permissions. Those guardrails govern what information an agent can use when making a decision.

Finally, governance should extend to the contextual layer, with clear ownership of the definitions, relationships, and business rules that determine how agents interpret information. These rules create a traceable path from source to context, making decisions easier to explain and validate.

AI readiness starts today

Making enterprise data AI-ready is a no-regret investment, as long as the work is tied to business value. AI can help accelerate that work. What delivers value today can also prepare the business for more advanced AI capabilities in the future.

Learn more here.

item.title: Microsoft expands sovereign cloud offerings as data control concerns grow
item.description:
Microsoft expanded its sovereign cloud offerings on Tuesday, adding new security, governance and AI capabilities as customers, particularly in Europe, demand greater assurance over where data is stored, who can access it and how critical services operate during disruptions.

The announcement builds on Microsoft’s ongoing digital sovereignty efforts, assisting organizations in applying appropriate levels of control to each workload rather than forcing a rigid, one-size-fits-all approach.

“Organizations are considering more than where data resides. They also seek to understand who can access and operate their systems, how sensitive digital assets remain protected, which technology dependencies matter most and whether critical services can continue as regulatory, geopolitical, security or network conditions change,” Douglas Phillips, president and CTO at Microsoft Specialized Clouds, said in a blog post.

The developments come amid growing international scrutiny of how global tech providers handle sensitive data and the extent of control customers retain over their digital infrastructure.

“Three factors are driving this, including stricter data regulations, rising geopolitical tensions, and growing AI adoption,” said Pareekh Jain, CEO at EIIRTrend & Pareekh Consulting. “Governments and enterprises want greater control over where their data is stored, who can access it, and whether critical systems can operate during disruptions. For instance, governments and big enterprises in Europe are worried about keeping their important data on an American company’s computers. Europe has proposed a new law that would limit the use of US cloud companies for sensitive government data in many areas. Microsoft is responding to these concerns while competing with local sovereign cloud providers.”

New controls across cloud and AI workloads

Microsoft is introducing the Sovereign Control Panel, a unified Azure portal experience that will allow organizations to assess their sovereignty posture, identify risks and gaps, apply controls, and evaluate workload portability. The panel is scheduled to enter public preview at Microsoft Ignite.

Expanding on Azure Key Vault Managed Hardware Security Module (HSM), which gives customers dedicated protection over encryption keys, Microsoft is now extending control beyond its own infrastructure. External key management with Azure Managed HSM is now generally available, enabling organizations to keep root encryption keys in hardware they own and operate on-premises or through a trusted third party.

In limited preview, Azure Confidential Clean Rooms will use confidential computing to support collaboration involving sensitive data, where participants will be able to analyse shared information while limiting broader exposure of the underlying data.

Microsoft is also expanding Azure Local to bring more cloud capabilities into customer-operated environments. The ability to transition workloads between connected and disconnected states is entering public preview. Additionally, DocumentDB and Blob Storage are entering public preview on Azure Local, while SQL Server on Azure Local is already generally available for connected and disconnected deployments.

On the AI front, Foundry Local is scheduled to become generally available at Microsoft Ignite for connected and disconnected operations on Azure Local. It will support local inference and agentic retrieval in natural language, backed by an expanded model catalog from Microsoft, partner networks, and the open-source community.

To further protect data during processing, Confidential Virtual Machines on Azure Local is now generally available, leveraging hardware-encrypted memory and isolation alongside workload attestation before sensitive keys or data are released.

While these additions give enterprises greater flexibility, industry analysts emphasize that localized deployments do not automatically erase vendor dependency.

“Depending upon the deployment model, in the public cloud, enterprises get better visibility, stronger access controls, and more control over encryption keys,” said Ashish Banerjee, senior principal analyst at Gartner. “In the Sovereign Private Cloud, they can operate infrastructure locally and even disconnect selected workloads from Azure. But I would not call this complete control. Enterprises still need to check whether Microsoft remains involved in identity, software updates, management, or technical support for the services they use.”

European oversight and partner options

For customers in the EU and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), Microsoft is rolling out Data Guardian. Under this model, a trusted regional partner will provide independent oversight of remote access requests by Microsoft engineers. Simultaneously, a Production Touch Ledger will create tamper-evident logs of all technical actions performed.

Microsoft is also broadening its Sovereign Partner Ecosystem, highlighting regional operators like Bleu Cloud in France and Delos Cloud in Germany, alongside independent software vendors specializing in security, identity, observability, and backup.

Geopolitical realities and market limits

Despite these additions, analysts note that technical controls cannot eliminate geopolitical dependence entirely. US hyperscalers (Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) continue to account for roughly 70% of the European cloud market, whereas European providers’ market share has contracted over the last decade.

The new measures introduced under Microsoft Sovereign Cloud do reduce risks but cannot eliminate them. “Local infrastructure, independent encryption keys, and disconnected operations make it harder for external parties to access data or disrupt services. However, Microsoft remains subject to applicable US laws, sanctions, and export restrictions. Enterprises gain greater operational independence but not complete legal or technological independence,” added Jain.

Furthermore, while sovereign cloud capabilities can offer greater control over data, infrastructure, and operations, this often comes with trade-offs in cost, performance, scalability, and access to services.

Banerjee noted that sovereignty should be assessed workload by workload, rather than applied as a label to the entire cloud environment. Greater sovereignty generally comes with greater cost and responsibility. Local or disconnected environments may not receive every Azure service at the same time. Enterprises may also need dedicated infrastructure, specialist skills and separate continuity arrangements. On top of that, they may lose some elasticity and economies of scale.

“So, I would not recommend maximum sovereignty for every workload. Reserve it for workloads where the legal, operational or geopolitical risk genuinely justifies the additional complexity,” added Banerjee.

item.title: Autonomy creep: how AI quietly gains more authority than CIOs intend
item.description:
Few CIOs are likely to suddenly decide to give an AI agent broad authority over corporate systems. The more likely path to autonomy is far less dramatic. An agent starts with a narrow task. It proves useful, so another system is connected. It then needs more data, so another permission is added. Then human approval becomes a bottleneck, so the organization removes it, and exceptions that once went to people start being handled automatically.

Each decision may be sensible in isolation. Taken together, however, they can leave an agent with considerably more authority than anyone originally envisioned.

That’s the danger of autonomy creep. And as enterprises move from AI systems that recommend actions to agents that execute them, CIOs need to govern not only what those agents were originally designed to do, but what they have gradually become capable of doing.

It starts with small permissions

Jim Taylor, president and chief product and strategy officer at identity security company RSA, sees a familiar pattern. Organizations typically create an agent for a specific purpose and give it the permissions necessary to accomplish the task. Later, the job expands.

“They just give it tasks, permissions; it just sits there and accumulates things,” he says. “Over time, it develops potentially toxic combinations. It gets too much access and can see too much data. It can do too many things.”

RSA

Humans accumulate permissions, too, of course, but organizations have developed processes around employees joining, changing roles, and eventually leaving. Agents may not have the same natural lifecycle. “They never give permissions back,” Taylor says.

Nancy Wang, CTO of 1Password, argues that CIOs should treat each expansion in an agent’s responsibilities as something more consequential than another feature. “Every time you expand the scope of the agent’s effective authority, you’re essentially adding a new authorization boundary,” she says.

That distinction between capability and authority is important. An agent may be technically capable of accessing a system, changing data, or executing a transaction, but that doesn’t mean the enterprise should automatically authorize it to do so.

Success can weaken oversight

Ironically, autonomy creep often occurs when AI works well. Paul Dongha, head of responsible AI and AI strategy at NatWest Group, sees that potential at the bank.

NatWest deployed agents in complaint handling, he says. Parts of the workflow that involve retrieving information from systems can be automated relatively easily, while humans continue to make the final decision on whether to uphold or reject a complaint.

If a system consistently produces the correct result, human reviewers may begin treating approval as a formality. The organization may eventually decide that the check is no longer necessary. “The temptation is to give over to the AI because it’s so reliable,” Dongha says.

NatWest sometimes reduces checking when an AI system demonstrates sufficiently high performance, he adds, but the decision is deliberate rather than incremental. It involves stakeholders and risk managers, and the system continues to be monitored afterward.

That’s a critical distinction for CIOs. Removing an approval step doesn’t necessarily represent poor governance. Removing it because everybody has gradually stopped paying attention to it does.

The warning sign is when a human moves from making a meaningful decision to merely rubber-stamping one — and then entirely disappears from the workflow without anyone reassessing the authority the agent has gained.

Put the controls outside the model

As agents acquire more authority, CIOs can’t rely solely on the agent to respect instructions about what it should and shouldn’t do. At 1Password, Wang advocates what she calls verified loops. Before an agent begins work, humans define its task, which tools it may use, what evidence will demonstrate that it completed the task successfully, and which actions it should never perform.

A separate verifier then compares evidence from the agent’s actions against that human-defined policy. “What you want to avoid here is something recursive where you have a fox guarding a henhouse, or the agent looking over its own work,” Wang says.

1Password

The principle applies beyond software development. A model might be instructed never to transfer more than a certain amount of money, delete a production environment, or access particular data. But if violating that rule would have serious consequences, the limit should also exist outside the model.

RSA’s Taylor makes the same distinction from the identity and access side. “Model-level guardrails are necessary, but not sufficient,” he says. “The real limits need to sit outside of that in enterprise control.” He argues for layered controls around agents, including identity policies, provisioning rules, lifecycle policies, governance, monitoring, and attestations.

In other words, CIOs shouldn’t ask an AI agent to exercise restraint where the infrastructure could simply prevent the unauthorized action.

Govern access in real time

Traditional access governance often operates on a schedule. A manager might review an employee’s permissions quarterly and determine whether those permissions are still appropriate. Agents may evolve too quickly for that approach. “Agentic identities are dynamic,” Taylor says. “So we need a mechanism that certifies them continuously, rather than performing periodic reviews.”

If an agent suddenly gains access to another database, for example, that event itself could trigger reassessment. Organizations should determine whether the new permission is appropriate or creates a dangerous combination with access the agent already possesses. “Privilege and authority should never be permanent,” Taylor adds. “They should always be reviewed.”

Wang favors an even more granular approach of task-based authorization. Rather than giving agents standing access or long-lived credentials, organizations can make authorization decisions at runtime and provide short-lived credentials only when required for a particular task. “We espouse no standing privileges,” she says. “No long-lived credentials.”

That effectively applies least privilege at agent speed. A change in task becomes an opportunity to reassess whether the agent still needs the access it’s requesting.

Make someone own the agent

Technical controls, however, don’t eliminate the organizational question of accountability. Taylor believes enterprises should be able to associate agents with a responsible identity. If an employee creates an agent, the organization needs to know who’s responsible for it, what its purpose is, and what happens to it if that person changes roles or leaves. “Every agent action needs to be attributed to a responsible identity,” he says.

Ownership also needs a lifecycle. An agent that remains important after its creator leaves should be transferred to another designated owner rather than simply continuing indefinitely.

Dongha makes another distinction. For AI embedded in a business process, he believes the business owner should remain accountable because that person owns the customer relationship, the process, and often the P&L. “It’s the business owner who has the responsibility because their people run it, and they’re responsible for the customer relationship,” he says.

That creates a useful division of roles for CIOs: IT may provide the infrastructure and controls, but the business can’t outsource accountability for the consequences of autonomous decisions.

Multi-agent systems need system-level controls

The challenge becomes more complicated when agents begin working together. An individual agent might remain entirely within its permitted scope while contributing to an overall outcome nobody intended. One agent generates an output. Another accepts it as input and takes an action. A third agent then acts on the result. Again, the individual actions may all appear legitimate.

Dongha says enterprises therefore need to test not only individual agents but the entire network as a system. “You need something overarching on top of a multi-agent system,” he says.

NatWest Group

NatWest is working on an AI control tower that would give authorized users visibility into a network of agents, including messages passed among them and the guardrails surrounding those interactions. Dongha considers governance of multi-agent systems an emerging problem that nobody has fully solved yet.

Wang also points to a related challenge that identity becomes more complicated when agents are ephemeral. An organization may spin up a temporary team of agents, tear it down, and recreate it later. If something goes wrong, the enterprise needs to reconstruct which agent made which decision during which session, and how that action propagated through the system.

That makes traceability increasingly important as autonomous systems become less like individual applications and more like networks of interdependent actors.

Set the bar before the agent reaches it

Before an agent goes into production, Taylor says CIOs should be able to answer several basic questions: Who owns it, what can it do, what’s its maximum authority, how will the organization know if that scope changes, and which actions require a human decision.

Other industries don’t need to replicate the governance machinery of a large bank, but they can borrow one important principle: controls should be built into the system from the beginning. “Governance shouldn’t be a check at the end,” Dongha says. “It needs to be embedded when you build an AI system.”

For CIOs, that may be the central lesson of autonomy creep. The question isn’t simply whether an agent can be trusted today but whether the organization has mechanisms to notice when tomorrow’s agent has quietly acquired authority that nobody ever intended to give it.

item.title: Building a trust architecture for your new team
item.description:
CIOs bring a lot to their new jobs: decades of leadership, transformation, pattern-recognition, and outcomes. But none of that matters in your new job. During a time of generalized uncertainty, your team — and every stakeholder — needs to trust you more than anything. But how do you build that trust in a new environment, and as quickly as possible? For Cengage CIO Ken Grady, the best approach is an architectural one.

What is a trust architecture, and why did you develop it?

I’ve been a CIO for almost 20 years, and when I joined Cengage six months ago, while I had roughly 7,300 days of evidence that I knew how to do this job, not one person in that building had ever seen any of it. The proof existed on my résumé. The trust did not.

On day one as a new CIO, you have no shared experience with your team, so you have no trust. Your team might have respect for your background, and hope you’ll succeed, but personal trust is something you must build from scratch.

So how do you do that when the currency of trust for your team can shift depending on the situation? Establishing trust with the people in your new business requires an intentional approach, an architecture.

What are the different currencies of trust?

The first is technical currency. My team needs to know that as a new CIO, I’ll respect their technical expertise, have enough of my own to be helpful, and engage in healthy technology discussions. To solve for that, I sat down and led an open conversation early on about whatever was on their minds, and I showed them that their technical expertise is valued.

The second is investment currency. Can I, a technology leader, speak to ROI or NPV? Can I explain why we should invest in this technology, or address this technical debt, or move from this version to that one? My team needs to respect my ability to guide our investments.

The third is human currency, which addresses the questions people are afraid to ask. Why did we move our offices? Why are we incentivized this way and not that way? IT people are people, and they have non-technical questions.

Technical, investment, and human currency get exchanged in a cadence of conversations, and that cadence almost matters more than the content itself. People value leaders who are steady.

How are you using the trust architecture now?

People have questions when a new leader comes on board, and they need a safe place to ask them. That’s why we built a monthly Enterprise Architecture Review, an open meeting with no agenda where technical people talk through hard problems concerning what we’re trying and learning, what’s working, and what isn’t.

We’ve also built a monthly portfolio review called Steps-to-Green. We talk about the yellow and red projects, and how we can help each other move them to green. There’s no punishment in this room, only encouragement. If your product is yellow, that means you’re one step closer to green.

But the fear is wondering if it’s okay to say what you really think, so the senior leadership team holds a monthly anonymous Q&A. Ask us anything, what you’re worried, frustrated, or even angry about. We might not have all the answers, but we’ll try. If you give your team that kind of safety, they’ll use it.

What’s the benefit of this safety?

You get a high-functioning team willing to challenge existing norms and continuously improve. There’s no such thing as a perfect organization, and safety creates an environment where anyone can suggest an improvement, try it, test it, and report back.

What you get with safety is democratic governance. If there’s a quality problem, anyone in IT can hit the big red button to say we’re not doing this release, we have a quality problem. Anyone on the team can know more than I do about this technology, migration, or this HR issue, and hit the button.

It doesn’t mean there’s no bandmaster. I still need to lead the band since that’s my job as CIO. But the trombone player has to trust me enough to tell me we’re not playing it right.

What advice do you have for CIOs building a trust architecture in a generally anxious workforce?

I cure prosciutto in my basement. Every time I start a new one, I remind myself it takes 18 months, regardless of how many years I’ve been doing it. Trust doesn’t care about your résumé. It’s earned, not given. Before your next conversation, ask yourself if you’re building trust in the currency this person accepts, or the currency I’m most comfortable spending.

Empathy should be your lens. With my team, I show up ready to learn something, connect with them, not to perform leadership. With my stakeholders, I understand they don’t care about my migration strategy. They care whether I’m making their life easier. With my board, empathy isn’t warmth. It’s precision on knowing they need confidence from me, not just an update.

Each direction takes a different currency for team, stakeholders, and customers. As a CIO, you can’t be comfortable in one lane and neglect the other two. You must invest in all three.

item.title: When everyone can build, the CIO’s job gets bigger
item.description:
For most of the last three decades, the technology organization’s authority rested on something simple: it held capabilities nobody else had. If the business wanted software, it came to IT. That arrangement no longer holds. A marketing team can now assemble a working customer-facing prototype over a long weekend using three AI tools, including some IT never evaluated, and the CMO can demo it Monday morning.

The common reading of AI’s effect on technology organizations is that engineers got faster. The more consequential reading is that the entire enterprise has become more capable – in a survey of 20,000 knowledge workers, 58 percent of AI users say they now produce work they couldn’t a year ago. Many will build without much regard for the estate their work has to live in. Meanwhile, the technology organization is still measured by uptime and cost to serve and is increasingly held accountable for the sprawling portfolio of AI tools used across the organization. The growing risk is that the technology organization is circumvented altogether, and core technology decisions migrate to people who now feel technically capable of making them, even if they don’t have the necessary context.

As the AI landscape evolves and brings more people into the technology conversation at a record pace, the CIO’s role shifts to cut through the noise. The new mandate expands on leading a sound technology strategy to providing increased clarity, rigor and disciplined judgment on where AI can catalyze growth. CIO-led initiatives should focus on compounding enterprise growth through AI, rather than allow a series of expensive experiments that distract and add bloat to an organization already on overdrive.

What has shifted

Build capacity grew, shifting IT’s focus from velocity to value

Increased technical capability has enabled teams to generate significantly more output, but product management, design, governance and stakeholder alignment have not scaled at the same rate. The constraint moved from the ability to build to the ability to align on what to build. To address this, we have seen some organizations add product managers to help rationalize demand, while others push product judgment to engineering teams, which often resurfaces as a sequencing discussion. Sometimes companies do both simultaneously, a sign that the question was never settled.

Automation moved up the value chain but never resolved the accountability question

A 1979 statement widely attributed to IBM held that “A computer can never be held accountable; therefore, a computer should never make a management decision.” Fast-forward nearly half a century, and systems now generate options, run variations and analyze outcomes at a pace that would have taken a competent analyst days. What they cannot do is be accountable for the result. A model can produce the recommendation, but it cannot be the name on the decision when a regulator asks. The work does not disappear as automation climbs; it concentrates into deciding and answering for it. AI automation is a technology and data question first, and technology leaders are best positioned to determine which decisions a model can safely make.

The SaaS reckoning is an architecture problem before it is a cost problem

A decade of SaaS tool proliferation has left most enterprises with overlapping applications and fragmented data, and the instinct is to hand rationalization to procurement and bank the savings. That instinct is expensive right now because the same fragmented estate that inflates license spend also makes enterprise AI underperform. An agent is only as good as its ability to get a consistent answer about a customer, and in most estates, there is no consistent answer to get. The accumulation of new, uncoordinated AI solutions risks compounding tech sprawl on an already fragmented foundation.

Separately, each is a familiar problem. Together they change the altitude at which the CIO org operates. IT’s response shifts from determining when something can be delivered to whether it should be built. IT identifies which decisions can be automated and which should remain in a human’s hands. Finally, the CIO’s team maintains the integrity of the enterprise’s estate by governing the pathways through which it evolves.

What only technology can hold

As the entire enterprise becomes more technically capable, IT’s role evolves to coach and advise where teams should build and how. IT might decide to build most things, partner only on select initiatives or federate altogether – but IT should maintain the keys to what enters the technology estate. While prioritization, accountability and architecture are not new concepts for a CIO and their team, today’s environment requires a different approach.

1. Judgment about what is worth building

Scarcity used to supply the discipline: when engineering capacity was the limit, prioritization was resolved through the queue. When a perfectly reasonable series of viable requests arrives, each with its own sponsor and business case, someone must maintain a position on what is worth building. This is a fundamentally different question for technology leaders to answer, and it puts strategy and enterprise capability ahead of capacity or technical capability. A PMO can sequence a list of projects and perhaps flag dependencies, but it cannot usually flag system incompatibility or tell you that something already exists two systems over. Technology sees all of it, which is the vantage point the strategic portfolio question requires.

Cheap to attempt is not cheap to own. While build cost may collapse, the cost of running, securing, supporting and eventually retiring a thing is not, and it is paid every year afterward by a team that did not choose it. The question was never whether it could be built. The discipline that maintains the estate’s integrity is declining things that are individually reasonable. This was easier when the answer was that there was no capacity. Now a “no” must be a judgment about the request itself, and that is harder to do when a seemingly viable demo already exists. This is technology’s to own, because only someone looking across the estate can see where the sum of sensible local choices stops working.

What to do: Identify the decision types that gate the most work in your organization; these usually involve data access, exceptions to standards and production promotion. Establish the standards that inform the judgment, then empower a cross-functional governance forum to apply them consistently. While most enterprises have or plan to have a forum, only about half have a formal process for approving AI work. Define that process and hold the entire enterprise to that decision logic, whether the answer is yes or no.

In operating model work with large matrixed organizations, the measure that moves leadership is decision latency. No one team owns the delay, so it never lands on any single scorecard. Measure it end-to-end and put the number in front of the executives whose calendars it is on.

What to measure: median days from question raised to decision committed; share of proposals declined, because a forum that approves nearly everything is sequencing the queue rather than setting the portfolio

2. Governance as a lever for enterprise speed

Across many enterprises, we have found versions of citizen AI development already underway, and ungoverned, before anyone had decided whether to allow it. IBM’s 2026 breach research found the share of incidents involving shadow AI more than doubled in a single year. The CIO’s role is to ensure AI experimentation and development occur somewhere visible, on supported foundations and with measurable outcomes. A clear process in place, assets available for reuse and a track record of enabling speed and scale give the business a reason to come to you first.

That makes speed of commitment the thing to design for. Enterprise speed is now set by how quickly the organization can align and commit, and most companies treat that as culture when it is a property of the operating model. Reaction time is the version the business feels: having watched a function stand something up over a weekend, it measures technology from request to outcome against what it believes it could have done itself.

What to do: Establish clear tiering that governs use case development based on risk, security, architecture and data impact, and be explicit about what the business may build, with what data and what must come through technology. Most people only need to use what has been published, a smaller group configures from approved patterns, and an even smaller group still builds things that write to production systems. Each tier carries its own training and its own standard of accountability, which is also where the line sits between what a model can decide on its own and what needs a person’s name on it, which most organizations still could not demonstrate under audit. Tiering earns readiness rather than granting permission, so work moves into the appropriate lane instead of being gated on the same criteria.

Then make the sanctioned path the fastest one and stock it with a component library, reference implementations, pre-cleared connectors and evaluation harnesses. Guardrails alone will not hold the line, because a control the business experiences as friction is an argument for going around it. And none of it works on publication alone, so treat enablement as part of shipping the path.

What to measure: share of new business-built solutions running on the sanctioned path; share of new builds drawing on at least one published asset

3. The digital harness the enterprise builds on

When everyone across the business can build, the question stops being who writes the code and becomes what all of it runs on. Security, privacy, data quality, automated testing and observability used to be properties of individual systems, owned by whoever built them, which usually meant IT. They now must be properties of enterprise platforms, supplied centrally and inherited by default. A dashboard built on published data shouldn’t be governed by the same policy as an agent that writes to a customer record, but each needs a clear pathway to its intended impact. Architectural coherence is achieved here as well, so that the same customer identifier retains its meaning across dashboards and autonomous agents alike.

Without a harness, IT’s bottleneck does not disappear when the business starts building; it relocates. That prototype ready to demo on Monday waits three months for a security review, a privacy assessment, a data quality fix and someone to write the tests and monitoring nobody considered at the start of the effort. Technology becomes the constraint again, only later in the cycle, more visibly and with less goodwill than it had when the queue formed before anything was built.

What to do: Build identity and access patterns that apply to anything the business stands up, quality thresholds on the data domains that matter most, testing written on the assumption that some code was machine-generated, and observability covering agents as well as applications. Align this with the tiers identified in the governance exercise so that efforts are right-sized for the initiative. The same foundation should govern what you retire, because rationalization decisions should lighten the architectural overhead as well as the license bill.

Then, resource the harness appropriately. Keep a person where the call requires judgment or where someone must be answerable for it, and let the rest run. Review, not build, is the scarce resource now, and knowledge workers already rank it first among the skills AI makes more important. Finally, develop talent proactively for review, as the repetitive work that built that capability is now being automated. Organizations that leave that to talent strategy rather than to the operating model will find their bench thin in three years.

What to measure: share of AI solutions meeting the production-readiness bar by default; share of critical data domains with a single system of record that everything reaches the same way

Start by writing the mandate down

Most of what is above takes quarters to put in place, but one thing can be done this month. Write down what the technology organization owns, what it enables, what it orchestrates with peers and what it no longer does, then work with the rest of the executive team to generate buy-in. Reduce ambiguity about IT’s role wherever possible.

The old model was simple: marketing had an idea, and IT built it. The emerging unmanaged model is just as simple: marketing builds it, and technology is asked to make it safe afterward. The ideal target is different: marketing still builds it, but on IT-enabled foundations that make it safe, scalable and supportable.

In Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index, organizational factors like culture, manager support and talent practices accounted for more than twice the reported AI impact of individual effort. The operating model will change either way, and what remains open is whether it changes by design and whether CIOs spend the coming decade shaping the enterprise’s AI agenda or executing someone else’s.

item.title: The CIO’s new recovery problem: Knowing what ‘good’ looks like
item.description:
For years, disaster recovery was built around a relatively simple question: How quickly can we get the business back online?

That question still matters. But for today’s CIO, it is no longer enough.

Enterprise technology environments have become too dynamic to define recovery simply as restoring applications, reconnecting infrastructure and resuming operations. Applications span on-premises infrastructure, cloud environments and SaaS platforms. Identities and permissions are constantly changing. Employees introduce new tools and automation into workflows, sometimes without IT knowing about them. AI is accelerating that pace of change even further.

As a CIO, I see this complexity firsthand. My organization is navigating its own transformation while modernizing the technology that supports the business. One challenge I believe CIOs increasingly share is what I call “complexity sprawl,” the accumulation of technologies, applications, identities, integrations and processes that makes it increasingly difficult to understand what exists, how everything connects and, most importantly, what normal actually looks like.

That creates a different recovery problem. When something goes wrong, how do you know what you are actually trying to recover to?

Restoring a system does not necessarily mean restoring a trustworthy system. A compromised identity may still have inappropriate access. A configuration may have been changed. An attacker may have created another way back into the environment. A dependency may have shifted since the recovery plan was last tested. Getting everything running again is only part of the job. CIOs also need confidence that what they are bringing back is something the organization can trust.

Know what ‘good’ looks like before something goes wrong

That confidence starts with visibility long before an incident occurs.

Most large organizations do not operate within one neat technology environment. They have infrastructure accumulated over years, systems introduced through acquisitions, cloud services adopted by different business units, SaaS applications and legacy platforms that remain critical to day-to-day operations.

That complexity is not inherently bad. Much of it exists because the business evolved, and the technology evolved with it. The problem comes when an organization loses the ability to understand the environment as a whole.

I have seen how difficult it becomes to maintain a single source of truth as environments grow more fragmented. As a CIO, I do not want my team trying to reconstruct that environment for the first time while we are already managing an incident. We need that understanding before the pressure is on. What systems are critical? What depends on what? Who and what have access? What changed recently? If we cannot answer those questions while the environment is healthy, we are going to have a much harder time answering them during recovery.

That is why I view inventory and dependency mapping as recovery capabilities, not simply documentation exercises. CIOs need a continuously updated understanding of critical systems, applications, identities and dependencies. The goal is not to eliminate complexity. It is to make that complexity visible enough that we can distinguish the environment we intended to build from the environment that actually exists.

Recovery is a decision-making challenge

The challenge becomes even greater when you consider how much legitimate change occurs inside an enterprise every day. Employees change roles. Applications are updated. Permissions evolve. Automation executes actions across systems. AI tools and agents are introducing new workflows and interactions at an even faster pace.

Shadow IT is not new. CIOs have dealt with it for years. What has changed is the speed at which employees can now introduce technology into the business. Someone can adopt an AI tool or build an automated workflow without going through the traditional processes that might have given IT visibility into it.

I am navigating that reality in my own organization. I want people experimenting. I want teams finding better ways to work. The CIO cannot become the person who simply says no every time the business wants to try something new. But giving people room to innovate also requires maintaining enough visibility and governance to understand what is operating within the environment, what data it touches and what risk it introduces.

That matters enormously during recovery. When thousands of legitimate changes coexist alongside potentially malicious ones, you cannot assume the answer is simply to roll everything backward. You need to understand what changed, when it changed and whether that change belongs in the recovered environment.

This is where recovery becomes as much a decision-making challenge as a technical one.

One thing you learn quickly as a CIO is that some of the hardest decisions during an incident are not purely technical. Technology teams can tell you whether something can be restored. The harder questions are whether it should be restored, which systems need to come back first, what dependencies have to be in place and when the organization has enough confidence to safely resume operations.

Establish decision rights before the pressure is on

Those decisions cross cybersecurity, identity, infrastructure, cloud, data, applications and business operations. Restoring one system may depend on another. Reinstating an identity or permission may introduce risk elsewhere. Returning an application to production may have downstream implications for customers or business operations.

The CIO should not be making every one of those decisions personally. Our responsibility is to make sure the organization has established the priorities, ownership and decision rights necessary to make them quickly when the pressure is on.

That means asking difficult questions in advance. What does a trusted state look like for our most critical environments? Which systems and identities need to be restored first? What dependencies have to exist for them to operate safely? Who has the authority to determine whether an environment is trustworthy enough to return to production?

An active incident is the wrong time to answer those questions for the first time.

Test the organization, not just the backup

It is also why I put so much value on testing. I have spent enough time managing large technology environments to know that what is written in a recovery plan and what exists in the environment can diverge surprisingly quickly. Technology changes. People change roles. Applications are replaced. New dependencies emerge. A process that worked six months ago may rely on assumptions that are no longer true.

A meaningful recovery exercise therefore has to test more than whether a backup can technically be restored. It should test whether the organization can identify the right recovery point, understand its dependencies, make decisions under pressure and determine whether the restored environment can actually be trusted.

I also view testing as an organizational exercise. Do people understand their roles? Are escalation paths clear? Does the organization have the expertise necessary to make decisions quickly? Are critical dependencies documented, or does that knowledge reside primarily with a handful of employees?

The skills question is becoming increasingly important. One of the challenges I think about constantly is how quickly technology is changing relative to our ability to keep people current. That is difficult under normal circumstances. During a recovery event, a gap in expertise can quickly become an operational gap.

You can have the right technology and the right process on paper, but if the expertise required to execute that process sits with one or two people, you still have a resilience problem.

Testing exposes those weaknesses when the stakes are lower. It creates operational muscle memory and gives teams experience making the kinds of decisions they may eventually have to make under much greater pressure. In that sense, recovery is not a document sitting on a shelf. It is an organizational capability that has to be continually exercised.

Redefining what successful recovery looks like

I do not expect enterprise environments to become less complex. AI agents, automation and machine identities will introduce even more activity into environments that many CIOs are already working hard to understand. Businesses will continue adopting new technologies, modernizing legacy systems and connecting environments that were never originally designed to work together.

The CIO’s job is not to eliminate that complexity. It is to make sure we maintain enough visibility and control to manage it.

For recovery, that means understanding what exists and how it connects before an incident happens. It means knowing what is changing and whether those changes are legitimate. It means establishing ownership and decision rights before teams are operating under pressure. And it means testing whether the organization can actually execute the plan it has put on paper.

Speed will always matter. Every CIO wants to restore operations as quickly as possible when something goes wrong. But speed without confidence is not resilience.

Ultimately, the most important recovery question may no longer be, “How quickly can we get back?”

It may be, “How do we know what we’re getting back to?”

CIOs who can answer that question before an incident occurs will be in a much stronger position when something inevitably goes wrong.

item.title: US bans DeepSeek across federal agencies, putting AI supply chains under scrutiny
item.description:
DeepSeek has been dealt a huge blow in the US, even as it continues to innovate and keep pace with, or in some cases outperform, rival models from American labs.

The US Secretary of Homeland Security has issued an order banning all DeepSeek products and services from federal agencies. Government organizations must purge their IT systems of it within 60 days; those with “compelling justification” can make a case for exemption by written request to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) cited multiple concerns about the Chinese-hosted model, including data sovereignty, lax Chinese laws, and security vulnerabilities.

Analyst Erik Avakian, technical counselor at Infotech, understands the concern. “When organizations use any type of hosted AI service, they’re potentially sending intellectual property, confidential business information, or other sensitive data into an environment where they may have very little visibility or control over what happens to it,” he said.

Government concerns

According to a document published in the US Federal Register, all technology developed by China-based Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. will be banned from procurement by federal civilian agencies. This includes affiliated products and any third-party tools or software built using DeepSeek implementations.

Affected civilian executive branch agencies include the Departments of Treasury, State, and Justice; it does not apply, however, to private consumers, the general public, state/local governments, or Department of Defense (DoD) national security systems.

“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” the Order stated. To begin with, the company’s servers are located in the People’ s Republic of China (PRC), whose legal system grants “extensive authority” to government cyber and intelligence functions to access private infrastructure.

DeepSeek’s account generation process collects personally identifiable information (PII) and may also track and digitally fingerprint users, the Order asserted. Its prompt response process may result in the transfer of sensitive data to the PRC. This could give it “actionable intelligence” on US programs or individual users.

Further, the Order stated, DeepSeek models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities. DHS pointed to open-source security research published in February 2025 that uncovered many iOS mobile apps with multiple critical vulnerabilities.

Until the ban takes full effect, DHS advised agencies to mitigate risk by monitoring inbound and outbound data traffic, implementing enhanced logging and controls on data exfiltration, and detecting and flagging anomalous activity.

Agencies can submit requests for exceptions to the ban in writing, and must provide a “compelling justification,” such as its impact on mission-critical functions, or other considerations related to national interest such as national security reviews, investigations, or security agreements, as reasons why such exemption should be granted,.

Security issues are rampant

The ban comes just as DeepSeek is open-sourcing DeepInfer, its in-house interference framework. DeepInfer powers DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with what the company said is high throughput and low latency. It features high-performance kernels, an optimized inference engine, structured outputs, and speculative decoding.

DeepSeek said its production token encoding and decoding components, which are aligned with processing logic behind the DeepSeek API, will bring the “same API behavior to community deployments.”

“Open models. Open kernels. Open inference,” DeepSeek posted to social media site X. “From private deployments to public clouds, we’ll keep working with the community to make large-scale inference more efficient.”

This isn’t its first roadblock from a cybersecurity perspective. Most notably, in January 2025, the company leaked more than one million log entries, including chat histories, API secrets, and other sensitive information, through an unsecured database.

DeepSeek reportedly addressed the exposure, but it still raised questions about the overall security practices surrounding the platform, particularly for organizations considering entrusting it with their own sensitive business information, Avakian pointed out.

That’s not to imply that every DeepSeek model is “inherently malicious,” he said, but there are still major questions around data privacy, the potential for information access under Chinese laws, the security of the broader AI ecosystem, and the susceptibility of DeepSeek’s models to jailbreaks and manipulation.

“Taken together, [these issues] raise legitimate concerns about whether organizations can adequately understand and manage the risks involved,” Avakian said.

Enterprises should seriously assess associated risk

Enterprises are increasingly exploring DeepSeek, although most publicly-documented adoption has been in China, Avakian noted. Some DeepSeek models have also been made available through platforms like Microsoft Azure and AWS.

“There’s genuine enterprise interest in the technology, as organizations look for opportunities to improve productivity, offer new capabilities, or reduce costs,” Avakian said. Useful applications include document summarization, internal research, and coding assistance.

DeepInfer also has the potential to reduce costs, but possible benefits should be weighed against associated security risks, he pointed out. The framework was just released, so organizations are going to need to validate the claimed efficiencies in their own environments rather than assuming savings will automatically translate into lower operating costs.

He encouraged organizations to start with relatively low-risk use cases, preferably using “public, synthetic, or appropriately sanitized information,” within a sandboxed environment they control themselves.

The important question to ask: ‘What is the business problem we’re trying to solve?’ From there, Avakian said, determine whether DeepSeek is the best way to solve it, validate security controls, and expand the use cases based on risk tolerance. Effective governance and risk assessment are key, he noted: understand what you’re bringing into your environment, validate its security, restrict its permissions, and make sure you can monitor what it’s doing.

“Approach this like any other software supply chain decision,” Avakian advised. “The fact that something is open source, inexpensive, or technically impressive doesn’t automatically make it appropriate for enterprise use.”

Impact on the broader AI ecosystem

The fact that the Order also addressed third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations is important, Avakian said, because organizations may be using DeepSeek technologies indirectly, through vendors, software platforms, or other services, without necessarily knowing what’s operating underneath. “These are classic supply chain issues,” he observed.

It’s no longer enough to know which AI applications employees are using; enterprises must understand which models, frameworks, dependencies, and external services are embedded in products they’re purchasing and deploying, Avakian said. This means revisiting AI inventories, potentially updating procurement requirements, and expanding processes around third-party risk management, he advised.

“Ultimately, enterprises leveraging these tools need to understand not only the AI technologies they’re intentionally deploying, but also the technologies they’re inheriting through third parties,” he said.

item.title: UK FCA exec wants to require disclosure of ‘significant AI failures and near-misses’
item.description:
When UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) Chief Data Officer Jessica Rusu gave a speech on Monday advocating that UK companies be required to report “significant AI failures and near-misses,” she added to the drumbeat of demands for some kind of regulatory control over enterprise AI deployments. 

But her speech also highlighted regulator frustration over futile attempts to slow down the seemingly unstoppable agentic and genAI rollouts, as reports of agent misbehavior and the lack of meaningful consequences continue to emerge with alarming frequency.

Rusu, speaking to a Bloomberg UK Policy Series audience, said that firms need to invest more in cyber and operational resilience.

“Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognized, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too,” Rusu said. “It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress, or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.”

She added, “the FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators, and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.”

One of the questions that came out of the speech is what precisely was meant by “significant AI failures and near-misses.” Questions to FCA to clarify their terminology were not answered by publication time.

AI failure vs near miss

But Pieter Arntz, a malware intelligence researcher at security firm Malwarebytes, offered his own take on what those terms likely mean.

“A significant AI failure is one with serious consequences, not simply an incorrect answer. In financial services, that could mean an AI system authorizing substantial fraudulent payments, exposing sensitive customer information, denying customers access to essential financial services, or triggering transactions that threaten market integrity,” Arntz said. “The test should be the scale and severity of the impact, rather than whether the failure looks technically dramatic.”

On the other hand, he added, “An AI near-miss is an event that could realistically have caused serious harm, but was caught before that harm occurred. For example, an AI agent might attempt an unauthorized transfer that a separate approval control blocks, or a prompt-injection attack might induce it to disclose sensitive information, only for an outbound security control to stop the disclosure.”

However, Arntz warned of the risk to Rusu’s approach, should the final penalties be underwhelming. “There is a risk of this becoming a paper tiger if compliance amounts to filing a report and absorbing a predictable fine,” he said. 

Warnings from multiple directions

UK-based Gartner VP analyst Nader Henein said he is skeptical about the significance of the FCA’s proposal, in part because so many UK enterprises already have to comply with EU regulations, which have started asking companies to make such disclosures.

“Financial watchdogs including the Bank of England (BoE), the UAE Central Bank, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore have all issued warnings,” he said. “A few months ago, the European central banks, together with the European Systemic Risk Board, escalated the cyber risk assessment level associated with frontier models to ‘severe,’ warning that simultaneous cyber incidents could impact the financial sector. They acknowledged that AI-driven cyber incidents now threaten core financial sector stability.”

Henein said that he is especially skeptical that meaningful changes will occur in the financial sector.

“Financial institutions tend to heed the warnings of the regulator that decides whether they can continue to operate, but without clear laws, regulatory oversight, and the obligatory fines, these disjointed statements are not likely to make a difference,” he said. 

Could ‘incentivize the wrong behavior’

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, added that one risk of this increased visibility requirement is that it could inadvertently incentivize the wrong behavior. 

“A bank with good monitoring may catch hundreds of attempts by AI agents to act outside their authority,” he said. “A bank with poor monitoring may report zero, because it never saw them. On paper, the safer bank looks worse. A model failing a red-team test is the test working, not a regulatory incident.”

However, Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, said that the near-miss approach has the strongest potential to change the conversation.

“I love the near-miss idea. It is the most important thing in the speech. It is the part financial firms are least ready for,” he said. 

But, he stressed, “[Rusu] also warns about reliance on a single model. An outage at one AI supplier that takes down a customer service channel counts, too.”

Another concern about reliance on a specific model is the ever-present risk that an AI vendor could change the model without telling all of its customers. 

“A model can pass testing in March and misbehave in May without anyone at the firm changing a line of code, because the provider changed the model underneath,” Dickson said. “A model version change should get the same scrutiny as any other production change.”
